title: A novel temporal recommender system based on multiple transitions in user preference drift and topic review evolution
research_question: Can a temporal recommender that jointly models multiple transitions in user-preference drift, time-based forgetting, and evolving review topics improve recommendations under changing preferences and sparse ratings?
methodology: The authors propose MTUPD, a temporal collaborative-filtering model that represents preference change through multiple latent-factor transitions rather than a single transition between time periods. It applies a forgetting-time function to reduce the influence of older interactions and uses nonnegative matrix factorization to extract evolving latent topics from review text, linking those topics with item factors in a joint objective. The model is evaluated experimentally against dynamic collaborative-filtering baselines on eight temporal recommendation datasets containing ratings and reviews.

key_findings.finding: MTUPD explicitly models user-preference drift across multiple successive transitions rather than treating temporal change as a single transition.
A forgetting-time function is used to attenuate the influence of older observations when estimating current user preferences.
Review text is incorporated through time-specific topic modeling so that evolving textual topics provide auxiliary information when rating observations are sparse.
The model jointly represents rating dynamics and review-topic evolution instead of relying only on timestamped ratings.
Experiments across eight datasets report that MTUPD outperforms the dynamic collaborative-filtering models used as comparators.
The approach provides evidence that explicitly modeling temporal preference transitions can improve future-preference prediction relative to the evaluated temporal baselines.

The paper does not provide evidence about explicit new, open, resolved, or superseded work-item states, calibrated uncertainty, reminder utility, or omission/repetition evaluation in longitudinal workplace briefings.

limitations: The evaluated task is recommendation from ratings and reviews rather than longitudinal workplace briefing or work-item state tracking.
The model represents temporal preference drift, but the accessible paper material does not describe explicit semantic lifecycle states such as new, open, resolved, or superseded.
The accessible material does not report calibrated predictive uncertainty, abstention behavior, or uncertainty presentation to users.
The accessible material does not describe evaluation of briefing omissions, unnecessary repetitions, or reminder value across repeated briefing cycles.

The publisher page did not expose the complete experimental section without subscription access, limiting verification of detailed hyperparameters, per-dataset numerical results, and ablation results.
raw_claims: Traditional collaborative-filtering methods have difficulty representing user preferences and item-related topics that change over time.
MTUPD models temporal user-preference evolution using multiple latent transition factors.
Older interactions are down-weighted through a forgetting-time mechanism.
The model incorporates review text to help compensate for sparse rating observations.
Nonnegative matrix factorization is used to identify latent review topics within different time periods.
User-factor transitions and review-topic evolution are incorporated into the recommendation model together.
The model links latent item factors with topic distributions as part of its joint formulation.
The authors evaluate MTUPD on eight datasets intended for temporal recommendation experiments.
The reported experiments show better recommendation performance for MTUPD than the compared dynamic collaborative-filtering approaches.
The paper's temporal state concerns changing user preferences rather than explicit lifecycle states of workplace tasks or communication items.
